introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores the complex property laws under the Hindu Succession Act (HSA), 1956. It dissects the concept of Coparcenary (Joint Family), the revolutionary 2005 Amendment giving daughters equal rights, and the specific rules of intestate succession.

core_concepts.title: Mitakshara vs. Dayabhaga Schools
core_concepts.description:
Hindu property law was historically divided into two schools:
- Mitakshara (Applies to all of India except Bengal/Assam): Property rights in the joint family are acquired by **Birth**. The son gets a share the moment he is born.
- Dayabhaga (Applies in Bengal/Assam): Property rights are acquired by **Death** of the father. No son has a right in ancestral property as long as the father is alive.

core_concepts.title: Coparcenary and the HSA 2005 Amendment (Section 6)
core_concepts.description:
A 'Coparcener' is a person who acquires an interest in joint Hindu family property by birth. Historically, only males up to 4 generations formed the coparcenary.
- The 2005 Amendment: The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 revolutionized this. Section 6 was amended to declare that a **Daughter of a coparcener shall by birth become a coparcener in her own right in the same manner as the son**. She has the same rights and liabilities in the coparcenary property as a son.

core_concepts.title: Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020)
core_concepts.description:
A massive jurisprudential landmark resolving confusion over the 2005 amendment. 
- The Dispute: Did the father have to be alive on Sept 9, 2005 (when the amendment passed) for the daughter to claim a coparcenary share?
- The Judgment: The Supreme Court ruled that the daughter's right is **retroactive** (arising by birth). It does NOT matter whether the father was alive or dead on Sept 9, 2005. Daughters have an absolute equal right to ancestral property.

core_concepts.title: Intestate Succession for a Hindu Male (Section 8, HSA)
core_concepts.description:
When a Hindu male dies without a will (intestate), his self-acquired property devolves sequentially:
1. Class I Heirs (Simultaneous, equal shares): Son, Daughter, Widow, Mother, etc.
2. Class II Heirs (If no Class I heir is alive): Father, Brothers, Sisters, etc.
3. Agnates (Relatives wholly through males).
4. Cognates (Relatives not wholly through males).

core_concepts.title: Intestate Succession for a Hindu Female (Section 15, HSA)
core_concepts.description:
The rules for a female dying intestate are different, prioritizing the source of the property:
- General Rule: Devovles upon (a) Sons, daughters, husband -> (b) Heirs of husband -> (c) Mother/Father.
- Exception: Property inherited from her Father/Mother goes back to the heirs of her father. Property inherited from her Husband/Father-in-law goes back to the heirs of the husband.

important_entities.name: Class I Heirs (Schedule of HSA)
important_entities.key_fact: The Mother is a Class I heir, but the Father is a Class II heir.
important_entities.significance: A highly tested exam trap. When a Hindu male dies, his Mother inherits an equal share alongside his widow and children immediately. His Father gets nothing unless the entire Class I list is empty.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Advanced exams mix up property types. A father can leave his **Self-Acquired Property** to anyone he wants through a Will (Testamentary Succession), completely ignoring his sons or daughters. However, he CANNOT will away his entire **Ancestral Coparcenary Property**; he can only will away his specific undivided fractional share in it.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: The sequential flow of Section 8. Property only flows to the next level if the previous level is completely empty.

exam_strategy_tips: If a Judiciary question asks 'Did the Supreme Court rule that the father must be alive on the date of the 2005 HSA amendment for the daughter to inherit?', select **NO**, citing the *Vineeta Sharma (2020)* judgment.
